Daniel’s “true equation → equilibrium describer” move is genuinely clarifying, but it risks sliding past a central distinction: in finance, the statement “tangency portfolio weights = market portfolio weights” is not a metaphysical equality so much as a theorem inside a very specific model class. In the CAPM story, it drops out of equilibrium only after piling on strong assumptions (mean–variance investors, identical beliefs, frictionless trading, etc.); relax them and you don’t merely get “temporary deviations that get restored,” you often get *a different object entirely* (multiple risk factors, segmented markets, limits to arbitrage, heterogeneous expectations), so there may be no unique “reset” target. Put differently: the blog treats equilibrium as a stabilizing force in time, but the result shown in many intro finance courses is primarily a *comparative-static equilibrium characterization*, not a guarantee about dynamics or convergence. That’s a subtle but important blind spot because it’s exactly where real markets—and many real physical systems—hide their complexity. A good anchor here is the original CAPM lineage Daniel is implicitly channeling: [Sharpe’s CAPM](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1964.tb02865.x) and its equilibrium logic.

The physics analogy is fruitful, but it needs a sharper fork: some “laws” are plausibly emergent regularities under coarse-graining (thermodynamics from statistical mechanics is the textbook case), while other “laws” are better understood as consequences of deep symmetries rather than equilibria. Conservation of energy and momentum, for example, are tightly linked to time-translation and space-translation invariance via [Noether’s theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noether%27s_theorem). That doesn’t make them untouchable—if the relevant symmetries don’t hold globally, conservation can fail in the naive sense—but it does mean “equilibrium” is not the only, or even the main, explanatory template. If Daniel wants a cleaner bridge, the more precise framing is “many macroscopic regularities are *effective laws* that depend on the level of description,” a theme developed in [Anderson’s “More is Different”](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.177.4047.393).

Finally, the time-travel aside illustrates the cost of keeping “equilibrium” too metaphorical. A cellular automaton can be deterministic or not; adding a “fifth dimension” and “injecting energy” doesn’t, by itself, specify constraints that would permit consistent backward causation rather than paradox. In physics, the hard part is not imagining extra degrees of freedom; it’s stating the dynamical rules and consistency conditions (e.g., whether closed timelike curves are allowed, what global constraints apply, and how information is prevented from producing contradictions). Without that, “equilibrium in 5D” functions more like a narrative patch than an explanatory mechanism—interestingly similar to how, in finance, invoking “the market will restore it” can paper over the actual frictions that decide whether mispricings persist.
